image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Packed bubble chart / circle packing diagram**

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **hierarchical grouping / enclosure**: many small circles are packed into larger clusters by occupation group.
   - Uses **size encoding** for magnitude (bubble area/diameter).
   - Uses **color** to distinguish categories/groups.
   - Not faceted, not stacked, and not a small-multiples layout.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation group / job family (e.g., Education, Health care, Sales, Transportation) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped spatial enclosure/cluster; text labels; color/hue of circles |
| Specific occupation (e.g., Registered nurses, Cashiers, Office clerks) | Categorical/nominal | Individual circles; text labels |
| Number of workers / employment count (e.g., 3 million, 1.4 million) | Quantitative | Bubble size (area); numeric text labels |
| Color category (gold vs gray groups) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue |

Notes:
- There are **no visible axes**, so no x- or y-position variable is explicitly encoded as a measured data field.
- The spatial arrangement appears to support packing/grouping rather than encode a separate quantitative variable.

I notice that the graph separates frontline workers from essential workers and also groups occupations by field. There are more frontline workers than essential workers. Areas such as healthcare, food preparation and serving, and transportation have the largest amounts of frontline workers. Meanwhile, education and office and administrative support have the largest amount of essential workers. 

I wonder what specifically qualifies an occupation as essential or frontline. I also wonder if these terms are popularized due to the pandemic and other natural disasters. I also wonder what the infection rate and mortality rate is for each occupation and whether this affects vaccine priority and accessibility.  

This impacts me because I know people who are frontline workers and essential workers. With limited supply and increasing infection rate, the prioritization of who receives the vaccine is important. While frontline workers have greater exposure and are more likely to catch COVID, cases spread quickly among the general population. Public places, like schools, that are open are also vulnerable, and therefore those with educational jobs can be as susceptible as frontline workers. COVID has affected many families, especially those with members who are essential and frontline workers. Hopefully, with the distribution of vaccines right now, both spread and deaths will be reduced.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the occupation groups with the most frontline workers are the following: Health care, Transportation, and Food preparation and serving. The occupation groups with the largest amounts of essential workers are the following: Education, and Office and administrative support. I also notice that the graph depicts several types of jobs within each overall category. There are thousands of workers contained within even the smallest circles. Finally, it appears that there are more frontline workers than essential workers. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what constitutes a frontline worker and what constitutes an essential worker. Why is it that machinists are considered frontline workers and not elementary school teachers?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I personally know at least one person who works in almost every single one of the categories depicted in the graph. Many of the people I know who work within occupations deemed "frontline" have received vaccines or are planning to receive vaccines in the near future. Essential and frontline workers exist in every community (especially my own) and they are the first individuals receiving vaccines. Hopefully rates of infection within my community will decrease as a result.

comments.raw_comment:
Upon first glance, I notice that there are about the same number of essential bubbles as frontline bubbles. Now there appear to be more frontline bubbles that have a large population, so in terms of people, there are more frontline workers. I also noticed that there are a lot of specific professions that have been declared frontline positions, that I personally wouldn't view them as essential frontline workers. However, I also have to take into account my location and the intensity of the pandemic, as well as how strict we are about our COVID restrictions. 

Going a little off of my last thought, I can't help but wonder if these numbers could be significantly reduced if all the states were to abide by the same structured COVID regulations. It would also be interesting to see a similarly formatted graph of a different country that has strict quarantine rules and few COVID cases. 

I live in a small community, so this graph would likely have little to no impact on me or my community. It is however, interesting to learn more about. 

"How political conscience will decide your future"
